citation.title: A Note on Close Elections and Regression Analysis of the Party Incumbency Advantage

standing_assumptions:
The paper (Statistics, Politics, and Policy 2014; 5(1-2): 1–11; printed and PDF page numbers coincide) states two propositions about estimators computed from a data set of elections indexed by pairs $it$ (region $i$, election $t$). Everything below was read from the page images.
[Model (1), Section 3.1, p. 5] “We now prove that a variant of the RD estimator is exactly reproduced by an OLS regression that includes all $N$ elections. Consider a statistical model that would motivate the use of the OLS estimator: $$DV_{i(t+1)}=\alpha+\beta DemWin_{it}+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jX_{ijt}+u_{i(t+1)},\qquad(1)$$ where $DV_{i(t+1)}$ represents a dependent variable of interest in the $t+1^{th}$ election in region $i$, $DemWin_{it}$ is an indicator variable for whether or not the Democratic party won the $t^{th}$ election in region $i$, and $X_{ijt}$ represents one of $J$ control variables associated with election $t$ in region $i$.”
[Setting of Proposition 1, p. 5] “We now prove that, under suitable conditions, ordinary least squares estimation of the model in equation (1) will exactly reproduce the RD estimate, even if the model in equation (1) is not correct. Let $k$ (the bandwidth) be a number between 0 and 1. Supposing that only the Democratic and Republican parties contest each election, a set of sufficient conditions for estimator equality follow:”. The forcing variable is defined inside Condition 1 (p. 5): “$DemVot_{it}$ is the difference between Democratic and Republican vote share in election $t$ in region $i$.” Conditions 1–3 (p. 5) and the definitions of $\hat\tau_{RD}$ and $U_b$ (p. 6) are transcribed in full in P023-T11.
[Model (2), Section 3.2, p. 6] “We now consider OLS estimators of model (1) such that the control variables include a polynomial expansion of $DemVot_{it}$. We will demonstrate that such estimators will tend to approximate $\hat\tau_{RD}$ in large samples. Consider the special case of the model (1), $$DV_{i(t+1)}=\alpha+\beta DemWin_{it}+\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jDemVot_{it}^{j}+u_{i(t+1)}.\qquad(2)$$”
[Appendix B, p. 10] “Assume $$\mathrm{E}[DV\mid DemVot]=g(DemVot)\,\mathrm{I}[DemVot<0]+f(DemVot)\,\mathrm{I}[DemVot\ge0]$$ where $g()$ is continuous on $[-1,0)$ and $f()$ is continuous on $[0,1]$. Let $\alpha=\lim_{x\uparrow0}g(x)$ and $\beta=f(0)-\alpha$. Note that we have not assumed that $\beta$ has a causal interpretation.” Sampling, same page: “If the sample is drawn i.i.d. from a population $U$ with $\mathrm{Supp}(DemVot)\supseteq[-k,k]$, where $k>0$, then for large enough $N$, we have $\hat\beta_{OLS2}\approx\beta$.”
Not printed, and needed by a formal statement (each is the reading the validators used): (a) $DemVot_{it}\in[-1,1]$, a difference of two vote shares on the proportion scale: Appendix B works on $[-1,1]$ and the constant 1 in $J=2\lceil(1-k)/(2k)\rceil$ presupposes it. The Remark to Condition 3 and Section 4 give bandwidths in percentage points; 0.5 percentage points is $k=0.005$ (clarity note P023-N001). (b) Under the two-party supposition, $DemWin_{it}=1$ when $DemVot_{it}>0$ and $DemWin_{it}=0$ when $DemVot_{it}<0$. Section 3.1 states no convention for $DemVot_{it}=0$ (Appendix B writes $\mathrm{I}[DemVot\ge0]$); Proposition 1 does not depend on one, because $DemVot=0$ lies in the central bin. (c) The letter $J$ has three uses: the number of controls in (1); the value $2\lceil(1-k)/(2k)\rceil$ in Condition 2, the number of bin indicators; and the polynomial degree in (2). (d) $N$ is the number of pairs $it$ in the data, and $it\in U$ means that the pair $(i,t)$ belongs to the set $U$. (e) Nothing in Conditions 1–3 keeps a bin from being empty. The indicator of an empty bin is identically zero, so the OLS coefficient vector of (1) is then not unique, while the coefficient on $DemWin$ is the same in every least-squares solution; the factors $|\tilde U_j|^{-1}$ of Appendix A are to be read over non-empty bins only (clarity note P023-E006). (f) The definition of $\alpha$ presupposes that $g$ has a finite left limit at 0 (P023-A001, not confirmed as an error). (g) Both propositions concern the estimators $\hat\beta_{OLS}$, $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ and $\hat\tau_{RD}$ as functions of the data, and $\beta$ of Appendix B is the jump of the conditional mean at 0; no potential-outcome model and no causal assumption is part of either statement.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 2 with the assumptions Appendix B states for it (continuity of $g()$ and $f()$), as printed; the witness (uniform margins and one continuous $h$) is the settling validator's construction and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.statement:
Counterexample to ‘$J$ sufficiently large’ under continuity alone, with one fixed law and one fixed conditional mean (settling validator's construction; not in the paper). Let $X$ be uniform on $[-1,1]$, $D=\mathrm I[X\ge0]$, and for $J\ge1$ let $q_J$ be the $L^2$ projection of $D$ on $\mathrm{span}(1,X,\dots,X^J)$, $r_J=D-q_J$, $v_J=\mathrm E[r_J^2]$, $\kappa_J=\mathrm E|r_J|/v_J$ and, for bounded measurable $h$, $T_Jh=\mathrm E[r_Jh(X)]/v_J$.
Claims. (i) [Unbounded amplification.] $\kappa_J\to\infty$ as $J\to\infty$; precisely $\kappa_J=\tfrac4\pi\log J+O(1)$. (ii) [Norm.] For every $J$, $\sup\{T_Jh:\ h\text{ continuous on }[-1,1],\ h(0)=0,\ \sup|h|\le1\}=\kappa_J$. (iii) [One fixed $h$.] There exist a continuous $h:[-1,1]\to\mathbb R$ with $h(0)=0$ and $\sup|h|\le\tfrac1{12}$, and integers $J_1<J_2<\cdots$, such that $T_{J_m}h\ge m/4$ for every $m\ge1$. (iv) [Consequence.] Let $Y=\tfrac12+h(X)$ with this $h$. Then $\mathrm E[Y\mid X]=\tfrac12+h(X)$ is continuous, $Y\in[\tfrac5{12},\tfrac7{12}]$, Appendix B's assumptions hold with $g$, $f$ the restrictions of $\tfrac12+h$, $\alpha=\tfrac12$ and $\beta=f(0)-\alpha=0$, and the population coefficient on $D$ in the least-squares regression of $Y$ on $(1,D,X,\dots,X^J)$ is $b_J=T_Jh$. Hence $b_{J_m}\ge m/4$ for all $m$, $\limsup_{J\to\infty}b_J=+\infty$, and $b_J$ does not converge to $\beta=0$; while the population RD difference $\mathrm E[Y\mid0<X\le k]-\mathrm E[Y\mid-k<X<0]\to0$ as $k\to0$. (v) No such $h$ is Lipschitz (by P023-T8(c)).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: regression (2) and Proposition 2 (pp. 6–7); Appendix B's assumptions and its $g$, $f$, $\alpha$, $\beta$, $h$ (p. 10; transcribed in P023-T12). Defined by the validators and not in the paper: $q_J$, $r_J$, $v_J$, $\kappa_J$, the functional $T_J$ (so that $b_J-\beta=T_Jh$, P023-T7(b)), and the reading of ‘sufficiently large $J$’ as a statement about the limit of the population coefficient $b_J$ for one fixed law (P023-E002/doubt/artifact/derivation.md, sections 1 and 8).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact facts on which the construction rests (P023-E002/doubt/artifact/derivation.md, sections 2, 3 and 6; none is printed in the paper). (1) $\mathrm E[r_Jp(X)]=0$ for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most $J$, so $T_Jp=0$. (2) $|T_Jh|\le\kappa_J\sup|h|$, and $\kappa_J\ge2$. (3) For uniform $X$: $v_J=c_n^2/4$ with $n=\lfloor(J+1)/2\rfloor$ and $c_n=\binom{2n}{n}/4^n$, and $\frac1{\pi(n+1/2)}\le c_n^2\le\frac1{\pi n}$ for $n\ge1$; so $v_1=\tfrac1{16}$, $v_7=\tfrac{1225}{65536}$. (4) [Gliding hump, exact inequality (19).] If $J_1<J_2<\cdots$ and polynomials $p_1,p_2,\dots$ satisfy $p_m(0)=0$, $\sup_{[-1,1]}|p_m|\le1$, $\deg p_l<J_m$ for all $l<m$, $\kappa_{J_m}\ge6m4^m$ and $T_{J_m}p_m\ge\kappa_{J_m}/2$, then $H=\sum_{m\ge1}4^{-m}p_m$ converges uniformly, $H$ is continuous, $H(0)=0$, $\sup|H|\le\tfrac13$, and $T_{J_m}H\ge4^{-m}\kappa_{J_m}/2-\kappa_{J_m}4^{-m}/3=\kappa_{J_m}4^{-m}/6\ge m$; take $h=H/4$. (5) Polynomials with zero constant term are dense, in the supremum norm, in the continuous functions on $[-1,1]$ vanishing at 0, which with (ii) supplies the $p_m$. The analytic input is (i), proved in section 5 from the Legendre expansion of $r_J$: $\mathrm E|r_J|=\frac{\log n}{\pi^2n}+O(1/n)$.
canonical_claim.note: Source: the settling validator's derivation at the highest effort (doubt.json: ‘Continuity alone does fail for one fixed uniform law and one bounded continuous h with h(0)=0; the derivation also proves kappa_J=(4/pi) log J+O(1)’), sections 5–6, equations (18)–(19). The rating of P023-E002 rests on it (‘for uniform margins there is a continuous h for which the coefficient does not converge to the jump as the degree grows’). The $h$ is produced by a recursive choice and is not given in closed form; a formalization may prove existence. Only the unboundedness of $\kappa_J$ is needed for (iii); the rate in (i) is stronger than necessary, and a formalizer who proves $\sup_J\kappa_J=\infty$ by another route has proved what (iii) uses. For uniform $X$ the event $X=0$ has probability zero, so $\mathrm I[X\ge0]$ and $\mathrm I[X>0]$ agree almost surely. The earlier validators (v1, v2) did not have this result and say so; their record that no fixed-law failure was established is superseded by doubt.json. The exact values $v_J=c_n^2/4$ were checked for $J=1,\dots,8$ when this list was fixed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix B, the step ‘$\mathrm E[u|DemVot]\approx0$ and therefore $\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}]\approx\beta$’, and the Remark to Proposition 2, as repaired by Sol: the exact identity for the coefficient error and its bounds
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P023-E002, smallest_repair), first sentence and the sentence on a fixed degree, verbatim: “Replace the Appendix B inference by b_J-beta=E[r_J(h-p_J)]/v_J, with |b_J-beta|<=kappa_J||h-p_J||_infinity and <=||h-p_J||_2/sqrt(v_J). … For a claimed fixed-degree tolerance t, separately require |E[r_Jh]|/v_J<=t, or sufficiently kappa_J times the smooth-part uniform polynomial error <=t; replace negligible additional fitted-model MSE gain as a sufficient criterion.”
Written out in full. Let $(X,Y)$ be random variables with $X\in[-1,1]$ ($=DemVot$), $D=\mathrm I[X\ge0]$ ($=DemWin$), $\mathrm E[Y^2]<\infty$ and $\mathrm E[Y\mid X]=\alpha+\beta D+h(X)$ with $h$ bounded and measurable. Fix $J\ge1$, let $\mathcal P_J=\mathrm{span}(1,X,\dots,X^J)\subset L^2(P_X)$, $q_J$ the $L^2$ projection of $D$ on $\mathcal P_J$, $r_J=D-q_J$ and $v_J=\mathrm E[r_J^2]$. Assume the second-moment matrix of $(1,D,X,\dots,X^J)$ is positive definite, so $v_J>0$, and let $b_J$ be the coefficient on $D$ in the population least-squares regression of $Y$ on $(1,D,X,\dots,X^J)$.
(a) $\mathrm E[r_Jp(X)]=0$ for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most $J$; $\mathrm E[r_J]=0$; $\mathrm E[r_JD]=v_J$; and $b_J=\mathrm E[r_JY]/v_J$.
(b) [Identity.] $b_J-\beta=\dfrac{\mathrm E[r_Jh(X)]}{v_J}=\dfrac{\mathrm E[r_J\{h(X)-p(X)\}]}{v_J}$ for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most $J$.
(c) [Bounds.] With $\kappa_J=\mathrm E|r_J|/v_J$, $|b_J-\beta|\le\kappa_J\,\sup_x|h(x)-p(x)|$ and $|b_J-\beta|\le\|h-p\|_{L^2(P_X)}/\sqrt{v_J}$ for every such $p$.
(d) $\kappa_J\ge2$.
(e) [Exact specification.] If $h(X)=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jX^j$ almost surely, then $b_J=\beta$.
(f) [Fixed-degree criterion replacing the Remark.] For $t>0$: $|b_J-\beta|\le t$ if and only if $|\mathrm E[r_Jh(X)]|\le t\,v_J$; it holds whenever $\kappa_J\inf_{\deg p\le J}\sup_x|h(x)-p(x)|\le t$, and whenever $\inf_{\deg p\le J}\|h-p\|_{L^2(P_X)}\le t\sqrt{v_J}$.
(g) [Finite sample.] Let $x_1,\dots,x_N\in[-1,1]$, $d_i=\mathrm I[x_i\ge0]$, let the matrix with rows $(1,d_i,x_i,\dots,x_i^J)$ have full column rank, and let $\tilde d$ be the least-squares residual of $d$ on the columns $(1,x,\dots,x^J)$. Then $\sum_i\tilde d_id_i=\sum_i\tilde d_i^2>0$ and $\hat\beta_{OLS2}=\sum_i\tilde d_iy_i/\sum_i\tilde d_i^2$; and if $\mathrm E[y_i\mid x_1,\dots,x_N]=\alpha+\beta d_i+h(x_i)$ for every $i$, then $$\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}\mid x_1,\dots,x_N]-\beta=\frac{\sum_i\tilde d_ih(x_i)}{\sum_i\tilde d_i^2}.$$
(h) [Constants for uniform margins.] If $X$ is uniform on $[-1,1]$: $v_J=c_n^2/4$ with $n=\lfloor(J+1)/2\rfloor$ and $c_n=\binom{2n}{n}/4^n$. For $J=1$: $r_1(x)=\tfrac12-\tfrac34x$ for $x>0$, $v_1=\tfrac1{16}$, $\mathrm E|r_1|=\tfrac5{24}$, $\kappa_1=\tfrac{10}3$, $1/\sqrt{v_1}=4$. For $J=7$: $v_7=\tfrac{1225}{65536}$, $1/\sqrt{v_7}=\tfrac{256}{35}$ and $4.7642006857252250<\kappa_7<4.7642006857252260$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: regression (2) and $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ (pp. 6–7); Appendix B's representation $\mathrm E[DV\mid DemVot]=\alpha+\beta\,\mathrm I[DemVot\ge0]+h(DemVot)$ with $h(x)=[g(x)-\alpha]\mathrm I[x<0]+[f(x)-(\alpha+\beta)]\mathrm I[x\ge0]$ (p. 10). The printed step being replaced and the Remark are transcribed in P023-T12. Defined by the validators and not in the paper: $\mathcal P_J$, $q_J$, $r_J$, $v_J$, $\kappa_J$, $b_J$ (P023-E002/v1/artifact/derivation.md, section 1, equations (A)–(C); P023-E002/doubt/artifact/derivation.md, sections 2, 3 and 7, equations (2), (3), (6), (23)). ‘The smooth-part uniform polynomial error’ is $\inf_{\deg p\le J}\sup_x|h(x)-p(x)|$.
canonical_claim.note: Exact and non-asymptotic; this is the statement Sol puts in place of the printed inference, and all three raisers and both validators derive it. $v_J>0$ alone makes $b_J$ unique, so the positive-definiteness assumption can be weakened to $D\notin\mathcal P_J$ in $L^2(P_X)$. (d) follows from $\mathrm E|r_J|\ge\mathrm E[r_J(2D-1)]=2v_J$. In (g) no integrability of an unconditional expectation of $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ is asserted: Sol notes that Appendix B's unconditional ‘$\mathrm E[\hat\beta_{OLS2}]$’ would need the expectation to exist. The constants in (h) are from doubt/artifact/check_exact.py and exact_results.json; $v_1$, $v_7$, $\mathrm E|r_1|$, $\kappa_1$ and the formula $v_J=c_n^2/4$ for $J\le8$ were recomputed exactly when this list was fixed, and $\kappa_7=4.76420068572522508\ldots$ numerically (the artifact certifies the bounds with Sturm-isolated roots of $r_7$, which has four simple roots in $(0,1)$). With these constants a uniform approximation error $\varepsilon$ of $h$ gives a coefficient error of at most $\tfrac{10}3\varepsilon$ at $J=1$ and $4.7643\varepsilon$ at $J=7$ for uniform margins; the multiplier depends on the law of $DemVot$ (P023-T5) and grows with $J$ (P023-T6). The criterion in (f) concerns the approximation error of $h$, not the further gain in fit of the fitted regression, which can be negligible while the coefficient is far off (P023-T4).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 2, as repaired by Sol and the settling validator: a fixed law with a density bounded below near the cutoff and a Lipschitz smooth part
canonical_claim.location: p. 7 (PDF p. 7); proof in Appendix B, p. 10 (PDF p. 10)
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P023-E002, smallest_repair), the sentences on Proposition 2, verbatim: “A sufficient minor primitive repair for Proposition 2 is a fixed law supported on [-1,1], with no atom at zero and dominating c dx on [-delta,delta], c,delta>0, globally Lipschitz h with h(0)=0, i.i.d. finite-second-moment sampling, bounded local conditional variance, k_N->0 and Nk_N->infinity; use fixed J for each target tolerance or a slow J_N rule (24) for simultaneous consistency. Then b_J->beta.”
Written out in full (P023-E002/doubt/artifact/derivation.md, sections 4 and 8). Hypotheses. (H1) $(X_i,Y_i)$, $i=1,\dots,N$, are i.i.d. draws of $(X,Y)$ with $X\in[-1,1]$ ($=DemVot$), $P(X=0)=0$, $D=\mathrm I[X\ge0]$ ($=DemWin$) and $\mathrm E[Y^2]<\infty$. (H2) There are $c>0$ and $0<\delta\le1$ with $P(X\in A)\ge c\,\mathrm{Leb}(A)$ for every Borel set $A\subseteq[-\delta,\delta]$. (H3) $\mathrm E[Y\mid X=x]=\alpha+\beta\,\mathrm I[x\ge0]+h(x)$, where $h:[-1,1]\to\mathbb R$ satisfies $h(0)=0$ and $|h(x)-h(x')|\le L|x-x'|$. (H4) $\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X=x)\le\bar\sigma^2<\infty$ for $|x|\le\delta$. (H5) $k_N\to0$ and $Nk_N\to\infty$. Notation: $q_J$, $r_J$, $v_J$, $b_J$ as in P023-T7; $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ is the OLS coefficient on $D$ in (2) at degree $J$; $\hat\tau_{RD}$ is the difference in means over $U_b=\{i:-k_N<X_i\le k_N\}$.
Claims. (a) For every $J\ge1$ the second-moment matrix of $(1,D,X,\dots,X^J)$ is positive definite, and $v_J\ge\dfrac{c\,\delta}{4(J+1)}$. (b) For every $J\ge1$ there is a polynomial $p_J(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\gamma_jx^j$ (no constant term) with $\sup_{x\in[-1,1]}|h(x)-p_J(x)|\le\dfrac{4KL}{J+1}$, where $K=\dfrac{3(1+\pi^4)}{4\pi}$. (c) [Population.] There is an absolute constant $C$ (the validator proves $C=8K$) such that for every $J\ge1$, $$|b_J-\beta|\le\frac{C\,L}{\sqrt{c\,\delta\,(J+1)}},$$ hence $b_J\to\beta$ as $J\to\infty$. (d) [OLS at fixed degree.] For each fixed $J\ge1$, $\hat\beta_{OLS2}\to_pb_J$ as $N\to\infty$. (e) [RD.] The population difference $\tau_k=\mathrm E[Y\mid0<X\le k]-\mathrm E[Y\mid-k<X<0]$ satisfies $|\tau_k-\beta|\le2Lk$ for $0<k\le\delta$, and $\hat\tau_{RD}\to_p\beta$. (f) [Proposition 2, corrected.] For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $J_0$ such that for every fixed $J\ge J_0$: $\hat\beta_{OLS2}-\hat\tau_{RD}\to_pb_J-\beta$ and $|b_J-\beta|<\varepsilon$. (g) [Degree growing with the sample.] Let $\lambda_J>0$ be the smallest eigenvalue of the second-moment matrix of $z_J=(1,D,X,\dots,X^J)$. If $J_N\to\infty$ and $\dfrac{(J_N+2)^2}{N\lambda_{J_N}^3}\to0$, then, with $J=J_N$, $\hat\beta_{OLS2}-b_{J_N}\to_p0$ and therefore $\hat\beta_{OLS2}-\hat\tau_{RD}\to_p0$; such sequences $J_N$ exist.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: Proposition 2 and regression (2) (pp. 6–7); $\hat\tau_{RD}$ and $U_b$ (p. 6); Appendix B's $g$, $f$, $\alpha$, $\beta$, $h$ and its i.i.d. sampling sentence (p. 10); all transcribed in P023-T12 and the standing assumptions. Formal reading of the printed ‘$\approx$’ and of ‘sufficiently large’ (the settling validator's; derivation.md, section 8): claim (f). Defined by the validators and not in the paper: $q_J$, $r_J$, $v_J$, $b_J$ (P023-T7), $\tau_k$, $\lambda_J$, and the constant $K$, which comes from the first absolute moment of the Jackson kernel $K_s(t)=A_s^{-1}\big(\sin(st/2)/\sin(t/2)\big)^4$, $A_s=(2s^3+s)/3$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact identities and inequalities the proof rests on (P023-E002/doubt/artifact/derivation.md; none is printed in the paper). (1) [Section 2, (2)–(3)] $b_J-\beta=\mathrm E[r_J\{h(X)-p(X)\}]/v_J$ and $|b_J-\beta|\le\|h-p\|_{L^2(P_X)}/\sqrt{v_J}\le\sup|h-p|/\sqrt{v_J}$ for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most $J$ (P023-T7). (2) [Section 3, (6)] for $X$ uniform on $[-1,1]$, $v_J^{\mathrm{unif}}=c_n^2/4$ with $n=\lfloor(J+1)/2\rfloor$, $c_n=\binom{2n}{n}/4^n$, and $c_n^2\ge1/(4n)$ for $n\ge1$. (3) [Section 4, (8)] under (H2), for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most $J$, $\mathrm E[(D-p(X))^2]\ge c\int_{-\delta}^{\delta}(\mathrm I[x\ge0]-p(x))^2dx$, whence $v_J\ge2c\delta\,v_J^{\mathrm{unif}}=c\delta c_n^2/2\ge c\delta/(8n)\ge c\delta/(4(J+1))$. (4) [Section 4, (9)] with $H(\theta)=h(\cos\theta)$ and $s=\lfloor J/2\rfloor+1$, $\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|t|K_s(t)dt\le K/s$, so the convolution $H*K_s$ is a polynomial in $\cos\theta$ of degree at most $2s-2\le J$ within $KL/s$ of $H$; subtracting its value at 0 at most doubles the error because $h(0)=0$, giving $4KL/(J+1)$. (5) [Section 8] $\tau_k=\beta+\mathrm E[h(X)\mid0<X\le k]-\mathrm E[h(X)\mid-k<X<0]$; each side of the window has probability at least $ck$ for $k\le\delta$; a binomial count $n_s$ with mean $Np_s$ satisfies $P(n_s<Np_s/2)\le4/(Np_s)$. (6) [Section 8, before (24)] with $K_J=J+2$ and $M=\mathrm E[Y^2]$: $\mathrm E\|\hat G_J-G_J\|_F^2\le K_J^2/N$, $\mathrm E\|\hat t_J-t_J\|^2\le K_JM/N$, $\lambda_J\|c_J\|^2\le M$, and on the event $\|\hat G_J-G_J\|_{op}\le\lambda_J/2$, $\|\hat c_J-c_J\|\le\frac2{\lambda_J}\big[\|\hat t_J-t_J\|+\|\hat G_J-G_J\|_{op}\sqrt{M/\lambda_J}\big]$. Printed in the paper and still used: the representation $\mathrm E[DV\mid DemVot]=\alpha+\beta\,\mathrm I[DemVot\ge0]+h(DemVot)$ with $h(0)=0$ (p. 10).
canonical_claim.note: This is the repair that the rating adopts for Proposition 2 itself (repair cost: a minor regularity condition; ratings.json, P023-E002, doubt_settled: ‘b_J tends to beta at rate J^(-1/2) when the density is bounded below near the cutoff and h is Lipschitz’). The constant is deliberately not optimal; what matters is the rate, and a formalization that proves (c) with another explicit absolute constant is faithful to it. (H2) asks for a density bounded below only near the cutoff: no upper bound on the density is used, and the law may have atoms away from $[-\delta,\delta]$. (H4) holds automatically when $Y$ is a vote share in $[0,1]$. Continuity of $h$ alone is not enough (P023-T6), so the Lipschitz condition, or some other quantitative smoothness, is a real addition to the printed assumptions. The statement does not say that $J=1$ or $J=7$ is ‘sufficiently large’ in any application: at a fixed degree the coefficient error is governed by P023-T7(b)–(f), and the settling validator records that the adequacy of the linear and degree-7 controls of Table 1 cannot be determined from the paper. In (g) the rule is the validator's equation (24); a sequence exists because every fixed $\lambda_J$ is positive (choose $N_j$ increasing with $(j+2)^2/(N_j\lambda_j^3)\le j^{-2}$ and $J_N=j$ on $N_j\le N<N_{j+1}$). Part (e) for $\hat\tau_{RD}$ is the standard degree-0 rectangular-kernel consistency argument and uses (H2), (H4) and (H5); support containing $[-k,k]$ alone, as printed, does not give growing counts in the window, a point the audit considered under P023-A002 and did not confirm as an error because the paper invokes ‘the usual conditions for RD’. The bound in (b) and the kernel moment bound were re-derived by hand when this list was fixed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix A, proof of Proposition 1: the display after ‘Therefore,’, with the summation index corrected from $i\in U_b$ to $it\in U_b$
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed (p. 9): “When $DemWin_{it}=0$ or $DemWin_{it}=1$ for all $it\in\tilde U_j$, $Dem\ddot{W}in_{it}=0$. Therefore, $\hat\beta_{OLS}=(\sum_{i\in U_b}Dem\ddot{W}in_{it}^{2})^{-1}(\sum_{i\in U_b}Dem\ddot{W}in_{it}\,D\ddot{V}_{i(t+1)})$, the least squares estimator as applied only to observations in the interval covering the discontinuity (noting that $U_b=\tilde U_{J/2}$).”
Corrected (Sol's smallest_repair: “Write $\sum_{it\in U_b}$ in both sums.”), with every hypothesis. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 1, last paragraph (‘all flexibly specified … mathematically equivalent to studies of close elections’; ‘rely solely on data from close elections’), with Section 3.2, last paragraph, and Section 5, first two sentences, as printed
canonical_claim.location: p. 3 (PDF p. 3); p. 7 (PDF p. 7); p. 8 (PDF p. 8)
canonical_claim.statement:
Section 1 (p. 3): “In fact, we demonstrate that all flexibly specified empirical studies of the party incumbency advantage using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression are mathematically equivalent to studies of close elections. The mechanics of linear regression with a covariate control for vote share are such that the resulting estimates rely solely on data from close elections. It follows that any concerns about the study of close elections are equally applicable to regression analyses including the entire dataset of all elections. As a consequence, we argue that a focus on close elections is fundamental to the empirical study of the party incumbency advantage.”
Section 3.2, last paragraph (p. 7): “Thus, we have established that, under a variety of circumstances resembling real-world practice, the OLS estimator (as applied to the entire dataset) may either exactly reproduce or approximate the RD estimator of the party incumbency advantage. Since the RD estimator only uses information from close elections to estimate causal effects, it is also generally the case that the OLS estimator, when well-specified, will also only use information from close elections to estimate causal effects.”
Section 5 (p. 8): “We have demonstrated that OLS estimation of the party incumbency advantage may produce estimates that rely solely on data from close elections. The limitations of studying close elections to estimate causal effects – both in terms of bias and of external validity – are therefore equally applicable to regression analyses that include the entire dataset.”
Formal reading of the claim about data use (the validators'): for an OLS estimator of (1) whose vote-share controls are adequate, in particular for $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ of Condition 2 and for $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ of (2) when the polynomial is correctly specified, the estimate, as a function of the outcomes with the margins held fixed, takes the same value on any two outcome vectors that agree on the close elections $U_b=\{it:-k<DemVot_{it}\le k\}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: regressions (1) and (2), $\hat\beta_{OLS}$, $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$, $\hat\tau_{RD}$, $U_b$ (pp. 5–7); ‘well-specified’ and ‘flexibly specified’ are not defined in the paper. The Remark to Proposition 2 (p. 7) describes adequacy (“the model fit cannot be meaningfully improved by including additional terms in the polynomial expansion”), and Section 4 (p. 7) names a linear control and a degree-7 polynomial as specifications of this kind. The formal reading is recorded in validated.json, P023-E001, natural_reading: “The phrase 'only use information' naturally asserts data dependence, not merely a shared estimand.”
canonical_claim.note: The statement as printed, listed because P023-E001 is rated Major; it is headline claim P023-H3 and bears on P023-H4. Under the formal reading it is true for $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ of Condition 2 (Proposition 1; P023-T11, P023-T3(a)) and false for $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ with a correctly specified linear or degree-7 control (P023-T1, P023-T2; in general P023-T3(c)). The Section 5 sentence says ‘may’ and is true: the coarsened estimator supplies the asserted possibility (both validators). The words ‘mathematically equivalent’, ‘any concerns … are equally applicable’ and the transfer of the limitations ‘in terms of bias and of external validity’ are interpretive and are not Lean matters; the validators establish only that a common discontinuity target does not imply the same observation weights, and they do not show that the two kinds of estimator differ in causal scope. A formalizer should state the formal reading for $\hat\beta_{OLS2}$ and refute it by P023-T1, and state it for $\hat\beta_{OLS}$ and prove it by P023-T11.
